Seeing A Better Future For AI
Amir Husain, Forbes, 2020-01-24

I grew up during the 80s and 90s, the kind of kid who built his own computers late into the night and heard the dial-up modem’s tones as my personal anthem. During this time of great promise in mankind’s technological potential I remember watching early documentaries on artificial intelligence (AI). My experiences as a software programmer, patent-holding inventor and successful entrepreneur during the past three decades were fueled by this wide-eyed optimism of my youth. I still draw upon that feeling daily, but more than ever we need to see past it if we are to create the best possible future for AI, a technology I believe that will transform the world as we know it.

As more people are connected online, it is more obvious than ever that such blind optimism is as anachronistic as a five and a quarter inch floppy. It seems as if the price for global societies being connected at machine-speed is a fuller awareness of the human costs that such progress can impose—if we let it.

When leap-ahead bandwidth from 5G connectivity is increasingly paired with rising adoption of different kinds of AI, today’s technology-fueled travails are only going to get tougher to solve unless we do something now. Social media has gone from a space for building bonds to breaking apart societies in order to win elections and sell online ads. Smartphones, instant messaging services and other forms of instantaneous connectivity have created neurologically-tinged expectations of responsiveness that are a running source of anxiety, as if we are constantly looking up to check the sky for inbound meteors. Randomly activated smart speakers, embedded location sensors in our phones and a plethora of online tracking technologies fuel fears of each one of us of being watched and tracked by nameless entities. And when we make it through a day of such anxieties, what do we have to look forward to in the 2020s? Out-of-control weapon systems? Our jobs being lost to robots?

With all that technology can do for us, it is indeed a tragedy that this is where we find ourselves standing when we are beginning a new decade. Not only are we questioning whether technology will create beneficial outcomes for us, the more we use digital technology, the less optimistic we seem to get. A Pew survey conducted in 2018 indicated that respondents who used technology for more than five hours outside of work were 38% more likely to be pessimistic about the future. We are in the midst of a vicious cycle.

How did we come such a long way from the techno-optimism of the 80s and 90s? We imagined all the world's knowledge being accessible to each of us and marveled how magical the effects of that would be. We contemplated the workplace of the future, one where we could see colleagues and collaborators via real-time video links allowing us more time with family and less travel stress. We fantasized about having access to unlimited entertainment and personalized news and content suited just to our tastes. How amazing this would all be! While we achieved all these past visions, we hardly feel positive about them now. Why is this the case?

I am no born-again luddite with a stocked bunker in New Zealand, to be sure. I have given my everything to build a business around the transformative economic and social power of AI and am personally optimistic about technology to a great degree. In fact, it is my conviction in technology’s potential to create a better life for my children and grandchildren that makes me want to wake people up to the ways we underestimate the present—and future—risks of emergent technologies. But it also means the pain I feel is personal, as it is acknowledging my sorrow at the accounting of squandered opportunities and lost potential to do something transformational for humanity.

This may sound to some like an existential lamentation. It is not. It is at its heart a computer scientist’s practical-minded appeal to rediscover the sense of wonder in the potential for AI and related innovations to create the kind of world that is better connected, more humane and broadly prosperous.

There are several ways we can do this. Firstly, we must simply accept this is our moment of lost digital innocence but not let ourselves wallow in it; we need to comprehend that Western capitalism has gone past a digital point of no return, as profound as electrification globally transformed everything from family routines to manufacturing; with empathy and inspiration we need to examine how employment is going to fundamentally change in order to reimagine work; and we need to start preparing ourselves for the combined effects of technological progress on ourselves at a biological level.

Right now there are kids in basements or behind bedroom doors tinkering with block coding on Raspberry Pis and Arduinos, building workbench robots. Most likely, they have only started to experience the quotidian digital opportunism and rancor familiar to their parents. If we act, these children will have enough time so this next generation of tinkerers and inventors can hold on to their digital innocence as long as possible. Their next wave of worldchanging technological breakthroughs may one day result in a similar reckoning as the one I have gone through, but at least they need not reinvent the pitfalls of today. Let us once again think about using technology for things that truly matter. Things that are good.
